utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please be seated. You may have taken note of the fact that we do not have a court officer in court. There is no one from the Registry, but I don't believe that I should inconvenience the parties and myself by waiting longer. If we can all be here on time, so can the representatives of the Registry, and I will make a note of that. May I ask the transcript person to spell my name correctly. Thank you. You might want to correct already the spelling you made. Did you? I don't see it on my screen but I trust you. Okay. Well, I will myself call the case. We are meeting for a Status Conference in the case of Prosecutor against Brdjanin. I will now call for the appearance of the parties. The Prosecution please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honours, Katharina Margetts for the Prosecution together with Senior Appeals Counsel, Mr. Peter Kremer, and our case manager Ms. Lourdes Galicia. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm John Ackerman for Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, will you stand up, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Can you hear me in a language that you understand, Mr. Brdjanin. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour, I can understand and follow the proceedings in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Brdjanin. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: This is a Status Conference called in accordance with 65 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Rule 65 bis (B) requires a Status Conference to be convened within 120 days of the last Status Conference to allow any person in custody pending appeal the opportunity to raise issues in the relation thereto, including the mental and physical condition of that person. The last Status Conference in this case was held on 28 June 2006. Almost 120 days have now passed since that Status Conference. Mr. Brdjanin, at the last Status Conference, you asked whether you were entitled to have a copy of the filings in your appeal translated into your own language. I have checked with the Registry about this and they have informed me that you are only entitled to have decisions of the Tribunal translated, not filings made by the parties. This answer is not in your favour, but I did want to let you know that I have followed up on your question. In this regard, it is important to note that your counsel, Mr. Ackerman, can read the filings and communicate with you in regard to their content. Mr. Brdjanin, I would like to ask you if you have any issues that you would like to raise at this time, any problems or concerns regarding your mental or physical well being? THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before I tell you about my mental and physical well being, I would just like to express my regret about the wrong translation. I didn't ask about any submissions to be translated. What I actually wanted was to have a translation of the appeal, but since there was a mistake in the translation, I discussed this with my counsel what pertained to the appeal so I think that there was a misunderstanding here. Thank you very much for listening to me. As for my physical and mental well being, I am in a situation that is appropriate to my years and appropriate to the situation that I am in. As the saying goes in my country, I am keeping up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Brdjanin. Of course you are entitled only to translations of the decisions of the Tribunal. As you know, the Appeals Chamber has scheduled all our arguments in this appeal for the afternoon of Thursday, December 7th, and the full day of Friday, December 8th. The Appeals Chamber may soon issue a further order identifying what time should be devoted to what arguments and perhaps -- and to which parties and perhaps specifying the questions for the parties. Before concluding the Status Conference, may I ask counsel for the Prosecution and Defence whether there are other issues they would like to raise at this time. Ms. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARGETTS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. The only question I was about to raise was concerning any questions which Your Honour might have and you've already addressed that and we'd obviously very grateful to receive those questions as early as possible to focus our preparations. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Margetts. This is certainly our object. Our experience has been that listing the questions in advance in the Scheduling Order does make preparation for the oral argument easier for both parties, and I intend to do so. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have two matters. One pretty much directly related to what we just spoke about. It seems to me that in a case where we have filed very comprehensive briefs and are not permitted to make argument to you that would be outside those briefs, new argument, things of that nature, that a day and a half of time set aside to make our presentations and submissions to you is quite excessive, and I would strongly suggest that we could make the submissions in this case in a half a day of sitting and limit us to like a half hour to make an initial presentation to you and then spend the rest of the time responding to your questions because that's the heart of what really is -- goes on in these hearings. It makes no sense for us to stand here for a day and a half and read our briefs to you or paraphrase our briefs to you. You've read them, you know what they say, and we can't go outside them, so I think it would just be unproductive for the hearing to proceed that way. A list of questions, of course, would be extremely helpful because that way we would have a chance to reflect on and prepare our answers and give a comprehensive response rather than something coming off the top of our heads. The second thing I would like to bring to your attention is this: We were recently provided and alerted to a huge archive of material, much of which has potential relevance to the issues in this case. This was brought to our attention by the Office of the Prosecutor. They have recently acquired numerous archives from Republika Srpska which have been placed in the electronic disclosure system. In addition, we were provided with a few thousand pages, I would say, of material developed in other trials in this Tribunal that are relevant or potentially relevant to this case. As Your Honour probably knows, I am lead counsel in a category 3 trial that's also going on in this Tribunal at this time, so upon receiving that material, I immediately started the process of trying to get some persons assigned to the case to assist me in working through that material and determining whether any of it is of a nature that would need to be the subject of a motion presented to the Appeals Chamber. I think today finally after many technical problems, a lawyer from Banja Luka will be appointed to assist in this matter. Most of this material, all of it that comes out of the archives in Banja Luka, is in B/C/S so I'm of no value in going through it. I have Mr. Brdjanin looking through the spreadsheets that we were provided, and I will have this lawyer from Banja Luka then available to actually go through the documents themselves, the ones that are flagged as being maybe pertinent to this case. I've also asked for the assignment of a co-counsel who is also familiar with the issues in this case, but that matter seems to have become completely stalled, and I have no idea what will happen to it. In any event, all that puts me in a position where I can't say to you that we will really be ready to submit this matter to you on the 7th and 8th of December, and so what I would suggest very respectfully, Your Honour, I know that a lot of time has gone by but this is pretty recent material is that the Appeals Chamber consider giving us perhaps until the 1st of February to make a determination as to whether or not an additional presentation must be filed with you. Just the spreadsheets alone for the material that has been disclosed exceed a thousand pages, so just the little descriptions of each document is 1.000 pages of spreadsheets. Just going through those is an enormous task all by itself. And then if we have to select out of that a number of documents and go through those documents, which it's inevitable that we will, I can't imagine that we can actually complete that task before the 1st of February. And I'm trying to make it as short as possible because I know you don't and I don't want to delay this matter any longer than it's already gone. But I think it's important in the interest of justice that Mr. Brdjanin have the opportunity for counsel assigned to his case to at least look at this material and become familiar with it and determine whether or not it could affect the outcome of this case. I have taken pains to have persons assigned to the case who are very familiar with the issues so that nobody has to spend a bunch of time learning the Brdjanin case. Everybody I'm asking to be assigned who will be working with us on this have -- has previously worked on the case so they have knowledge. So I'm doing the best that I can to speed it up as much as possible, Your Honour, and we have run into some technical snags but I think it's now moving forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Let me understand, Mr. Ackerman, what is exactly in your mind, the significance of the date of 1st of February that you have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the only significance is that I believe that considering there's going to be a fairly large recess in December, that that would give us enough days between now and then to get through that material and make a determination as to whether we need to file an application with the Chamber for the admission of some additional evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: But do you have a problem with our having the hearing as scheduled?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if you have the hearings as scheduled, then we would be -- it may be that we would have to just do it over again and we could have a supplemental hearing if that would -- and that would of course work. We could have the hearings as scheduled and still make the filing and maybe have additional hearings at a later time after some additional briefing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Your 115 motions can be submitted even after the hearings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that. I just thought it might be more efficient to get the matter dealt with before the hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I understand. Let me hear the view of the Prosecution on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I would like your views, please, on the two matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. With respect to the first matter of limiting the time for the oral arguments, I'd just like to briefly raise one issue that we would like obviously the Chamber to use its discretion in light of any questions you might have that appropriate time will be given to the parties to address those questions, which might be more time than counsel has just suggested. And also there is a necessity for the Prosecution's appeal at least to make certain additional submissions, not outside of the issues dealt with in the briefs, but with respect to recent jurisprudence we'd just like to bring to the Chamber's attention, for example. So that's one matter. With respect to the disclosure of material --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Wait, wait, let us finish the first matter first. It has been the recent practice of the Appeals Chamber usually to fix one day for the appeal hearings. Out of the concern for the complexity of this case and the many issues that arise in this case, I felt that I should allow for a day and a half. Maybe in view of the fact that you do not really object to the suggestions made by Mr. Ackerman, what occurs to me is that we might, in our Scheduling Order, suggest -- proceed on the basis that we will hold hearings on Thursday afternoon and Friday morning and I would -- if the Bench is agreeable to that, and I will of course have to consult them, we would then keep Friday afternoon in the reserve, should something -- should it be -- become clear in the course of the proceedings that one of the parties or both require more time, we would then be able to give them a little bit more time. That will be acceptable to you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's a very sensible suggestion. I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Now, let us move on to the perhaps more complicated matter, the possibility at this late stage, the Defence may wish still to submit Rule 115 motions. I would like to hear the Prosecution on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. As I understand, the Defence has just raised three issues. One is the notification letter we have sent to the Defence, I believe couple of months ago, notifying them of an archive that has been collected in Banja Luka, and we have been informed by the local authorities that this archive was accessible to both the Defence and the Prosecution so that either party could go down there and search for material. There is limited documentary material that we brought back from that archive which has been placed on the EDS. From our initial review of that material, this -- a large amount of that material is not directly relevant to this case because it relates to east Bosnia, the Drina Corps, and Sarajevo, and those documents that are relevant as we can see from our initial review to an extent are old documents that have been collected from other places in the Republika Srpska and centralised in this new archive. So while we obviously have to wait for any additional evidence motion to be filed to be able to deal with specific documents that come up, we believe that not a large amount of new material would come out of this selection. And then the second matter Mr. Ackerman raised was in relation to the disclosure of transcripts and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Wait a second. It's not clear to me since when have the parties been aware of that -- the existence of that archive. Only from the time you wrote a letter, a notification to the Defence or did the Defence know about it earlier?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARGETTS
utterances.text: We are unaware of that. We have been informed of the existence of that archive, I believe, in June or July of this year, and members of the Prosecution's office and we know members of the Defence in other cases have been down in Banja Luka accessing this archive. And we have notified the Defence of the disclosure of documents on the EDS from that archive at -- on the 22nd of August, I believe, when the material was processed and placed on the electronic disclosure suite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So what has happened, assuming that this date is 22nd of August, Mr. Ackerman, have you been able since then or did you consult those records?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first thing I did was try to figure out what was there and what I needed to -- in terms of resources to be able to look at it. And so the first thing I did was just look generally at what had been made available. I must tell you, just being in total candid with the Court, I had heard earlier that there was an archive that had been opened up in Banja Luka and I made inquiry of an associate in Banja Luka about that and was told that he had made inquiries and that it was not true, that there was an archive that had been opened up and then when I got the letter from the Prosecution, I realised that there was one or at least that I was being made aware of it at that point. At that point, I then started trying to get a couple of people assigned to the case to look into that matter and I told you we ran into all kinds of technical problems. But that is now happening and our associate and -- that is being assigned probably today in Banja Luka has actually been in the archive and has been looking through and has actually found some documents. It may very well be the case, and it tends to me to be my feeling right now that among the thousands of documents, there would be very few that would have any relevance to this case, but the only way to make that determination is to at least do a cursory examination of what's available, and those from the east Drina Corps and Sarajevo and the Romanija Corps are prima facie, I suppose, not relevant, although any one of those documents could provide some significant new information about the way the chain of command operated in the army in Republika Srpska during the relevant time and may not. It's impossible to tell at this time. But I think February 1st is not an unrealistic time for us to be able to get through that material and I -- the Prosecution thinks there is very little there that may be of interest to us but it's that very little that I need to find and it's a bit like looking for a needle in a haystack in some ways but there probably is some material there that is useful and as -- we are working through it. The process is underway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. You still have a month and a half to the oral hearings, and I see no reason why it would not become clear to you within the next week or two whether there is something really important that would justify a 115 motion, and certainly you could try within next three weeks or so to submit such a motion if you are really convinced there is something in it which can help your client. I must tell you that while I will consult the Bench about the representations you have made, I certainly, as Presiding Judge, am not inclined to postpone the hearings, oral hearings in this case for such a long time. Mr. Brdjanin is entitled to a speedy trial. His day, he has been waiting for his day in court and to postpone that in the present situation where it is fairly iffy whether you really find something significant would really not be the right course to follow. And again, you still have quite a considerable time before the hearings. But again, I will consult on this, my colleagues and I will see how they feel. Back to the Prosecution now and the other remaining issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've got not much to add to that. I mean, we would agree, be favourable to us to proceed with the hearing as scheduled in light of the large amount of time. Now, I just wanted to briefly mention the disclosure of transcripts Mr. Ackerman has raised and clarify that a large amount of those transcripts related from -- from a related case, the Krajisnik trial that has just been completed, and I believe it was around 20 witnesses where portions of confidential transcripts were disclosed to the Defence and in our view it should be possible to identify in a fairly short period of time any material, if relevant, and most of the witnesses that we indicated to the Defence testified in open session and were available to the Defence. Thank you very much, Your Honour. That was all I had to say on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. I see Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just two things and then I'll be finished. What the Prosecution says about the transcript is absolutely true and correct. We can get through those rapidly; I'm not worried about those at all. I think we're probably maybe as much as halfway through them already, so that's not a big problem. With regard to the previous question about the date, I just want to reflect in the record that Mr. Brdjanin is not insisting on his right to a speedy hearing; in fact, it's his request that I am making today. He asked me to make a request that he be given and his Banja Luka counsel be given adequate time to work through these new documents and -- and it's his suggestion that the hearing be held off until February, so I'm just making that request on his behalf, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. The record will reflect the points that you have just made. If there are no other issues, I thank the parties for their attendance and call the proceedings to a close. I look forward to seeing you all at the oral argument and we will soon issue an additional Scheduling Order which will clarify the date and also the duration of the hearings. Thank you very much.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
